source_review.notes: Reviewed current Python iterator/data-model documentation, Rust Iterator/IntoIterator contracts, C++ iterator concepts and requirements, Java SE 25 Iterator/Spliterator contracts, ECMAScript iteration protocol, and the Go range specification. All ten final destinations returned HTTP 200.

evidence: Checked iterator transition notation, finite sequence notation, half-open ranges, size bounds, and split equations for consistent domains and terminal cases.
Distinguished yielded values, exhaustion, operational errors, close, cancellation, invalidation, and source mutation as separate protocol outcomes.
notation_and_syntax.notes: Capability terms are used as contract properties rather than inferred from surface method names.

evidence: Recomputed the executable trace: first=10, mutation invalidates the old iterator, snapshot remains (10,20,30), and a new iterator has remaining values (20,30,40).
Checked the array split example arithmetically: [0,10) splits at 5 into sizes 5 and 5 with union size 10 and empty intersection.
numerical_recomputation.notes: Finite traces test examples and do not prove all iterator implementations correct.

evidence: Re-derived the induction that repeated successful advances yield s_0 through s_(n-1) exactly once before stable exhaustion for the stated finite model.
Re-derived split coverage and nonoverlap for [lo,mid) and [mid,hi), plus order restoration by left-before-right concatenation.
Checked that map preserves cardinality/order, filter preserves relative order but only an upper size bound, take bounds an infinite source, and zip stops at the shortest source.
symbolic_recomputation.notes: The laws depend on stable source, callback, ownership, and error assumptions named in the chapter.

evidence: Reviewed empty, singleton, exhausted, repeated-next, valid sentinel-like values, infinite sources, fallible sources, and early abandonment.

Reviewed mutation before/after yield, version-counter wrap, structural versus element mutation, stale references/proxies, shallow snapshots, concurrent access, cancellation, callback exceptions, and resource cleanup.

Reviewed graph cycles, duplicate reachability, unstable traversal order, inaccurate size hints, partition imbalance, side effects under parallel execution, corrupt durable records, retry duplication, and hostile sizes.
boundary_and_adversarial_cases.notes: Fail-fast version checks are explicitly diagnostic and not a substitute for synchronization or memory safety.

evidence: Each successful next advances exactly once; completion is distinct from data and is stable for the fused model.
Traversal order, item ownership/lifetime, mutation policy, invalidation, errors, cleanup, and repeatability are specified as independent contract dimensions.
Recursive partitions preserve coverage, nonoverlap, valid bounds, remaining-size accounting, and required encounter order under the fixed-source assumption.
invariant_checking.notes: Snapshot topology does not imply deep immutability of yielded objects.

evidence: Reviewed the finite-sequence induction against initialization, successful transition, and terminal transition assumptions.
Reviewed the split argument using half-open interval union, intersection, and recursive induction.
Reviewed which conclusions fail when mutation, callbacks, concurrent effects, ownership, or cleanup assumptions are weakened.
proof_review.notes: The chapter gives scoped proof structures, not a mechanized proof of any language runtime or arbitrary implementation.

evidence: Proof obligations and derivations state their assumptions and are not presented as universal guarantees.

The durable-record and medication examples name the required systems, security, reliability, data-owner, clinical, safety, privacy, quality, human-factors, and regulatory review scopes without claiming those reviews occurred.
proof_sketch_labeling.notes: Exactly-once processing and deployment safety are explicitly conditional, not established by examples.

evidence: The Python snippet passed exact six-line stdout, empty stderr, zero exit status, and recorded the toolchain report under artifacts/snippets/DSE-008/.
The snippet labels its result evidence=finite_protocol_trace, and all ten cited source destinations were directly checked.
empirical_evidence_labeling.notes: No cross-language runtime, concurrent iterator, parallel speedup, resource leak, production stream, or clinical system was empirically evaluated.

conceptual_review.notes: Reviewed iterable/iterator separation, external/internal and pull/push control, single/multipass and capability refinement, state machines, traversal order, ownership/proxies, mutation/invalidation, lazy adapters, size hints, errors, close/cancellation, cursors, graph traversal, infinite sources, fallibility, partitioning, concurrency, evolution, and evidence boundaries.

practitioner_review.notes: Reviewed API contract questions, mutation policies, versioning limits, callback effects, resource lifetime, adapter cleanup, snapshot cost, compatibility, hostile inputs, model/property tests, fault injection, race analysis, partition tests, and durable-stream checkpoint/retry obligations.

pedagogical_review.notes: Builds on DSE-001 through DSE-007, develops one precise protocol model before language comparisons, counters common misconceptions, connects six adjacent programs, and provides ten worked examples plus five matched exercises and answers from foundational through advanced practice.

limitations: Internal authoring, source, mathematical, snippet, conceptual, practitioner, and pedagogical evidence only; no external language/runtime, compiler, concurrency, security, reliability, data-governance, medical, clinical, safety, privacy, regulatory, quality, accessibility, human-factors, or independent review is claimed. The chapter and finite evidence prove neither arbitrary implementation correctness, race freedom, leak freedom, exactly-once delivery, parallel performance, clinical safety, certification, nor deployment fitness.
